en: Then his soles tapped the earth,
Steam billowed from his head,
He cried out to the Creator.
Rich Jakyp stood weeping:
“I was asleep; it was a dream.
This was God's doing!”
When he sprang up, it was night;
For Jakyp at that time
It was a Night of Power.
The being who had spoken and gone
Was Kydyr himself.
“His name has become Manas,”
The anguished rich Jakyp
Had heard him say.
Hanging his belt around his neck,
At that moment rich Jakyp
Pleaded with the Creator.
The true dawn had appeared;
The stars of Taraza, one by one,
Had all set, not one remaining.
When Jakyp sprang up,
Dawn had broken clear,
Light had touched the earth.
When rich Jakyp sprang up,
The first of his acquired stock to breed,
The dun mare that had borne no foal—
His good fortune spread like ash,
That dun mare had borne a foal.
The dun mare taken as an omen
Had now borne a foal;
What she bore was no mere foal,
She had borne a mighty one.
The dun mare, first of the herd,
Had given birth this year;
When the dun mare gave birth,
She had truly borne a whirlwind.
“Look at him from every side,
His mane and tail cascade.
My precious Toruchaar,
His marks of a great steed are plain.
Look at every fine part of him,
His wondrous form is plain.
He has a tail, he has a mane,
Such a beautiful creature!
If Toruchaar survives,
He will be a surging, mighty steed;
Whoever asks for him will become a stranger.
Every limb stands distinct,
The creature's splendid conformation is plain.
If he lives to become a horse,
Until his lead-rope is worn to a handspan,
He will not yield to a determined enemy.
Unless misfortunes strike by thousands,
He will not let his rider be speared by the foe.
Hearing uproar, his limbs loosen;
Hearing a battle cry, the creature
Shows the marks of a great steed.
Unflustered when the ochogor gun fires,
Even hearing an earth-splitting uproar,
He never sets one foot wrong.
When given his head,
He leaves the other steeds behind.
Hearing a battle cry, the blessed creature
Shows the marks of a great steed.
Where he walks, the black earth
Splits layer upon layer.
Never slipping on the heights,
In nothing is he inferior
To a wild goat walking on stone.
Whoever rides him will be nimble;
If Toruchaar survives,
He will be a horse fit for a hero.
Hoe-like hooves, broad rump—
If Toruchaar survives,
He will be a horse to ride into battle.
A hardy, well-bred horse—
If Toruchaar survives,
He will be a horse to ride into combat.
A leopard among spearmen,
A skilled man will ride him;
One who will bring strife to the world,
A mighty man will ride him.
His fetlocks will not bend;
He is a horse like a warrior.
These are no ordinary mane and tail;
This precious Toruchaar
Is unlike any horse I have seen!”
He examined the foal;
In his joy, rich Jakyp
Looked at him once again.
As he looked at Toruchaar,
Wishing for the joy of livestock,
Toruchaar pawed the earth
And stamped upon it.
Over his mother,
Springing back and forth,
He was leaping.
Seeing this, rich Jakyp's
Heart grew troubled:
“Grant him a master to ride him!”
He prayed to God,
His heart grew troubled.
“If only He grants a son to ride him,
If only my eyes see him mounted,
Then afterward I may die,” he said.
When he saw Toruchaar,
He shouted, “Baabedin!”
And called his horse-herder.
His heart and ribs throbbed,
His chest rattled,
His whole body trembled.
Before he had closed his mouth,
Before he could say this or that,
From a spur of the dark mountain,
From a jutting promontory,
Dust surged up in billows.
Seeing the dust, rich Jakyp
Felt the life leave his body.
When he looked at the surging dust,
It was Telküröng's dust.
The rider mounted upon him
Was a man like Akbaltay.
Baltay came with news;
To rich Jakyp, barely able to stand,
He called for a reward for good tidings.
Akbaltay spoke these words,
Said this to rich Jakyp:
“Rich Jakyp, my child, a reward for good tidings!
Today, for your good fortune,
A hero, a hungry lion, has come!
Whom sorrow could not bring into our hands,
A leopard sultan, a hero, has come!
No one could withstand him;
In both hands he held menace.
He shouted while still in the womb,
He raised the battle cry, ‘Manas!’
The blue-gray ewe with yellow temples
Bore a yellow-headed ram.
When your Manas was born,
He came upright upon his feet!
Black blood in his right hand—
Khan Manas came forth grasping it.
His coming forth with black blood in his right hand
Meant, if there is an enemy to fight,
‘I shall make black blood flow,
I shall spill his blood.’
Yellow gold in his left hand,
His coming forth grasping it
Meant, if there is an enemy to battle,
‘I shall make him yellow as yellow gold,
I shall bring him to his end.’
When your child came from the womb,
The tips of his ears were pierced,
He was circumcised.
Those who saw him were distressed.
O my Jakyp, consider:
Your child who came from the womb
Had signs as great as these.
When the child came forth roaring,
Dust rose from where he landed.
At the child's crying,
Hearts leaped, lives fled.
They had seen what they had never seen.
‘He is no child, but a monster!’ they said.
Nine poor old women
Died of fright.
Those who saw him were shaken;
Upon your child's back,
A dark blue-black mane appeared.
When your Manas came to earth,
Light poured down and filled him.
The dark-maned leopard—
‘Let his name be Manas,’ they said,
And your child was named.
When the women went to wrap him,
There was this other sign:
A black-spotted leopard
Leaped at his side,
Over that newborn child
It stepped three times, back and forth.
When they looked, it was out of sight,
No one knew where it was;
It vanished into the unseen.
A blue-gray lion with a poker-like tail
Leaped on his right side.
When they saw the lion,
‘What horror is this?’ they said.
The women fled screaming,
All the people
Rose and fled in terror.
Of the newborn child Manas,
It sniffed the right shoulder once,
Sniffed the left shoulder once.
Growling and turning,
The champion and the lion
Lay together, poised.
Look once, and he is like a child;
Look again, and a gray tiger.
If he lives and grows,
No one who faces him will survive.
His forehead reached the earth,
God's light poured from the sky,
An earthquake began.
Your newborn son Manas
Is a servant beloved of God.
Look at each part of him,
He is a boy of ninety thousand lives.
If he lives and grows,
He will come of age and become a hero.
A dark-maned leopard,
He will be a lion full of wrath.
His tread will be burning coals,
His shot will be a steel bullet.
He has been named Manas;
There will be none like him in the world.
He is the lion named Manas.
We were driven into exile from afar;
Our Kyrgyz kinsfolk—
He is the hero who will find them for us.
He is the lion who will undo your grief;
He is the hero who will keep us free of sorrow.
He was born in Altai;
Know that the Night of Power has come.
Think upon it, Khan Jakyp:
Some good fortune will come to us,
The day has come.
What you wished before has come to you;
Today, matching your dream,
The event has come.
Rich Jakyp, the dream you saw has come true.
Chyyrdy has borne a son,
He has been named Manas.
Has such a thing happened among your people?!
His figure, his bearing,
His appearance at birth—
The dream you saw came very close.
Jakyp blessed by Kydyr, hear me:
Such a thing does not happen in the world!
Every sign of your child matched exactly.
Allah the Almighty,
By His own will, bestowed good fortune.
When he was born, the black earth
Could not hold still, but rocked.
The lion named Manas—
See, a hero has come to us!
My Jakyp,
Such a thing cannot be won by pleading;
A dream does not readily come true.
That the Creator should give a child like Manas—
Is such a thing remembered?!
He is marked out, he is our support.
This son of yours, champion Manas,
Is a lion to gird about your waist.
For fortune that lies bound,
He is the boy who will unlock it.
For people living in humiliation,
